52. **A hash in prose is untyped, and reading a tree as a commit produces a confident false correction.** I published `495a4d5f1b3` as the tree of the commit being pushed. The P0.5 session read it as a commit, found nothing above `3cadda3d54f` on origin, and drafted a note telling me my branch pointer was wrong — then ran `git cat-file -t`, got `tree`, and confirmed `rev-parse 3cadda3d54f^{tree}` matched it exactly. Every git object name lives in one 40-hex namespace, so nothing in the string distinguishes a commit from a tree or a blob, and the failure mode is quiet rather than loud: `rev-parse` resolves it happily, while `log` and `merge-base` reject it in terms that read as "not on this branch" — which is indistinguishable from the branch pointer being wrong. **Run `git cat-file -t` before treating a hash you did not produce as a commit, and name the type when publishing one.** This is rule 39's shape arriving from the other side within minutes of that rule being written: the disagreement was real, and it was a unit error rather than a defect.
53. **A battery's self-check is a checker, and inherits every failure mode of the checks it supervises.** Rule 46 asked *is there a verdict line* where the discriminating fact is *how many fired* — presence substituted for occurrence, which is rule 36's superset satisfying a check for a set and rule 36's bare `5` satisfied by the `4` heading the list it counts, now recurring inside the tool built to catch them. Nothing exempts the supervisory layer: run on it the checks you run on what it supervises. I then supplied the instance from the other end, while testing that very case — `$args` is a PowerShell **automatic variable**, so `function Run($label, $args)` bound nothing, `@args` splatted empty, and all four cases silently ran the same unperturbed invocation and returned an identical `PASS (12 prose claims)`, including two that must fail. Reading only the uniform PASS would have confirmed the defeated rule and shipped it. Count-equality catches this too — perturbed 1, fired 0 — which is a second and independent argument for preferring it: it constrains the result rather than enumerating the ways a harness can break, so it is the one assertion that survives a battery broken in a way nobody anticipated.
54. **A backtick is markdown's code delimiter and PowerShell's escape character, so writing board text through a double-quoted string silently destroys every code span in it.** Appending to P0.6's entry that way produced, from one line, `` `re.IGNORECASE` `` → `<CR>e.IGNORECASE`, `` `find_anchor` `` → `<FF>ind_anchor` and `` `theta` `` → `<TAB>heta`: measured on a 53-character sample, the double-quoted form came back **47 characters with zero backticks and one CR, one FF and one TAB injected**, each control character having eaten the identifier's first letter. Three things make it worse than an ordinary typo. The injected bare CR is a line terminator to `ReadAllLines`, so the line silently splits and `git diff` reports the file as a whole-scale rewrite — 682 insertions against 682 deletions — which sent me looking at line endings, the wrong layer entirely, and `i/lf w/crlf text=auto` all checked out fine. A trailing backtick escapes the closing quote, so the failure sometimes arrives as an unrelated parse error dozens of lines later; that happened twice while trying to demonstrate the effect, which is the demonstration. And nothing about the result looks wrong in a commit message or a summary, so it ships. **Use the `edit` tool for prose, or single quotes and `@' '@` literal here-strings when scripting it**; the four board commits made through the edit tool changed 2, 3, 2 and 6 lines, which is what a correct edit looks like. Caught only because the format contract's trailing-whitespace check ran afterwards and flagged a line ending in a space — a check written for a cosmetic rule catching a content-corruption bug, which is the argument for running the cheap structural checks even when the edit "obviously" cannot have broken them.
55. **A rule written here reaches nobody who needs it: a spawned session reads only its kickoff prompt, so a kickoff must name, by number, the rules its step will exercise.** Every kickoff this project has issued — P0.1 through P0.5 — cited zero rule numbers, because `## Operating rules` sits fifty-odd entries deep in a file a child has no reason to open, and none of them opened it. The cost is measurable in P0.5 alone: the child independently rediscovered the presence-for-occurrence substitution and the unanchored-grep hazard *after* both were written down here as rules 53 and 43, spending a round each on findings it could have been handed for free. Name the numbers rather than paraphrasing them, because a paraphrase is a second copy that goes stale on its own schedule — rule 46 was rewritten twice inside one day, first around count-equality and then bounded with a precondition and with the shipped gate's immunity, so a kickoff that had paraphrased its original form would have handed the child the exact version that same child had already defeated. The general defect is broader than kickoffs: an invariant parked in one step's entry binds that step and nothing after it, which is how both the anchor-uniqueness check and the rules-46/49/53/54 requirement began life as P0.6 habits rather than rules, and promoting them here is what makes them bind every later step instead of only the next one. This rule is that promotion applied to itself.
56. **The `edit` tool reports "File updated with changes" for a no-op, so an edit is confirmed by the diff, not by the tool's success message.** Removing a blank line before rule 55, I passed an `old_str` and a `new_str` that were character-identical — both began with a single newline where the fix required the search string to begin with two — and the tool reported success. The file was unchanged: `git diff` produced the identical hunk and, decisively, the same blob hash `08d8e39d1b9` before and after, which is the only signal that distinguished "the edit applied" from "the edit matched nothing that needed changing". This is rules 46 and 53 once more, in the tool used to write the rules themselves: a success report confirms the call was well-formed, not that the intended change occurred, exactly as an exit code confirms a checker ran rather than that it read the right document. The remedy is the same shape as count-equality — assert the *result*, not the report: read the diff after every edit, and prefer an `old_str` that spans the boundary being changed (here, the tail of rule 54 plus the blank plus the head of rule 55) over one anchored on a single side, because a one-sided anchor is what let an identical pair look like a valid edit. The same reading turned up a second instance beside it: the rule-numbering scan matches `^\d+\. ` line by line and so passed 55 rules with no gaps in both layouts, being structurally blind to the blank-line change it sat next to — a check answering a different question loudly, which is rule 43.
57. **Compression preserves figures while deleting the clauses that scope them, so every number carried through a rewrite must be re-checked against its new neighbours.** The P0.5 PR body was cut from 5,170 words to 432 on the user's instruction, and `5 files added, 13 modified` survived into a sentence introducing the *deliverable*, where it is wrong. Both numbers were right as computed: the PR adds 43 files and modifies 14, of which `P0.5-baselines/` is **38 added and 0 modified**, the harness is **5 added and 13 modified**, and `P0.4-harness.md` is the fourteenth. The figure had been measured for the harness and the compression removed the clause saying so, re-binding a correct count to the wrong subject. That is harder to catch than a wrong number, because nothing local contradicts it — the arithmetic is sound and the source is real, and only recomputing the named subject exposes it. It is rule 39 from the other side: there, a count that disagreed might still have been a unit nobody asked about; here, a count that agrees perfectly is reported about something else. The second half is the handoff. The rewrite arrived with an explicit list of eight figures to re-verify and five deleted strings to confirm absent, and all thirteen checked out exactly — because **a battery drawn up by the author of a change inherits that author's blind spot**, and the single defect sat in the one figure the list did not name. Verify what a summary *asserts*, not only what its author thought to flag; the items volunteered for checking are selected by the same understanding that produced the error. The implementer sharpened this afterwards and the sharpened form is the operational one: the list was not a battery that happened to miss a case, it enumerated the figures the rewrite **preserved**, so by construction it could not cover the one figure the rewrite **changed** — and changed is where the defect lives. **When reporting an edit, list what you changed and let the reader check what survived.** That turns a caution about blind spots into a testable instruction, and it explains why a wholly accurate list still gave false assurance: every item on it was true, and the set was chosen by the wrong criterion. My own confirmation carried the same shape one level down — I counted the deliverable with the pattern `docs/design/lxr-port/P0\.5-baselines`, which is unanchored at its end and so matches both the directory and `P0.5-baselines.md`; the total of 38 was right only because the sentence's subject happens to be the union of the two, and it took the implementer's `37 + 1` partition to show the looseness and the subject coincided rather than the count being right by construction.
58. **Verify the consequence, not only the mechanism: the mechanism decides whether a defect exists, the consequence decides what you do about it, and a report can be exactly right about the first and wrong about the second.** The implementer traced a real defect in `verify-baselines.sh` — `--results` selects which checkpoints are audited (`:149`) while every data check reads `$BASE` (`:249`, `:270`, `:288`), so the two halves of one comparison come from two roots — and I confirmed all of it by reading. Attached to it was the assessment that the unsafe case is a rerun whose checkpoint filenames match the committed ones, which "can pass while never reading what you pointed it at". That part is false, and it is the part that drives the decision: `rederive-statistics.py` places three unconditional `return 1`s before its single `PASS`, failing on `checked_mean == 0` when the join produces nothing (`:226`), on `unmatched_cells` for a partial join (`:229`) and on `mismatches` for a full one (`:232`), so every manifestation of a split root fails loudly and a silent pass needs a fresh run to reproduce the committed numbers within a 1e-4 tolerance across every mean field. The flag is **unusable, not dangerous** — which turns "interrupt the merge and fix it now" into "fix it as P0.6's first tooling change", the opposite action. Note also that the implementer's own demonstration, a decoy directory yielding `FAIL (28 passed, 2 failed)`, is evidence for the *safe* direction and was offered as evidence for the dangerous one; a demonstration confirms the mechanism it exercises, not the severity claimed around it. And `:226` is count-equality (rule 46) already shipped by the script's own author, arrived at independently, which is the strongest support that pattern has.
59. **A gate that only compares can only catch mismatches; nothing in it catches a smaller input set.** `verify-baselines.sh` builds its checkpoint list with `find "$RESULTS_DIR"` (`:149`) and contributes one `ok` per checkpoint inside the loop at `:244-259`, so a supplied directory holding a correctly-named **subset** yields `RESULT: PASS (30 checks)` at exit 0 where the full set yields 34 — every check honest, every number re-derived, two thirds of the evidence never examined, and the banner still reading `mode: full audit`. This defeats my own universal: I declined to treat the `--results` split as dangerous because a split root "fails loudly in every case I could construct", and all four of those cases turn on a **mismatch** — differing names, empty join, partial join, differing numbers — while this one contains no mismatch at all. The defect is absence of coverage rather than presence of a fault, and no comparison fires on an absence. That is rule 57 one level up, and it lands on the author of rule 58: I verified the consequence, then bounded it by an enumeration selected by the same model of the tool that produced the claim. The bound on the fix is the script's own design principle at `:10-11` — *"Expected counts are DERIVED from the artifact, never repeated as literals at several assertion sites, so two cannot drift from a third unnoticed"* — which is precisely why no literal `3` guards the input set: **the principle that prevents brittle assertions and the hole are the same fact**, the second time on this gate that an immunity and a defect have turned out to be one property. Note also what the author did reach: `:414` names-vs-present, `:449` citations-vs-resolved, `:502` committed-vs-recomputed, each comparing two derived quantities and printing the difference. Five arrivals at count-equality in one repository, and the input set still unasserted — because every one of them compares two descriptions of **the same set** (contents) and none asserts that it is **the right set** (extent). The fix that respects `:10` derives the expected count from the artifact too, comparing checkpoints found against checkpoints the document names, in the exact shape of `:414`. **Assert the extent of the input set, derived, or the verdict's scope is unasserted no matter how many of its contents agree.** Discharged against my own board battery the moment the rule was written, because it had the identical gap: it asserted phases, steps, rule numbering, whitespace and control characters — all *contents* — and never the size of the field set, so an edit that clobbered a `- **Status:**` line in a step I wasn't looking at would have passed every check. Measured: **360 fields parse, 358 of them inside the 54 steps, 0 steps missing `Status`, 0 missing `Summary`, 6 ≤ fields per step ≤ 10.** The literal `360` is the part that goes stale the moment P0.6 adds a step, so the standing invariants are the derived ones — *every step carries a non-empty `Status` and `Summary`*, and *the step-field sum plus the phase-level fields equals the total* — which hold at any size.
60. **When a discrepancy equals a structural count of the document, suspect the method before the artifact.** The implementer's `442` words against my `429` for one PR body differed by exactly `13`, which is the body's blank-line count. PowerShell hands multi-line command output back as an `Object[]` of lines — `gh pr view --json body --jq '.body'` returns **34 elements, not one string** — and `-split` applied to an array runs **per element**, so every blank line contributes one empty string to the total. Reproduced against the live body: naive split `442`, empties dropped `429`, `-join` then split `429`, `[regex]::Matches('\S+')` `429`, blank lines `13`, delta `13`. Note what identified the cause: not three methods outvoting one, but **the delta equalling a count the document already publishes**, which names the defect rather than merely outnumbering it. The underlying mechanism is this shell's array/scalar duality, and we hit it within the same hour **from opposite sides** — I wrote `$r57[0].Length` expecting a line and got `1`, because a single `Where-Object` match comes back as a bare string and `[0]` indexed a character. Assumed-array-got-scalar and assumed-scalar-got-array, one duality, one session. The guard is to force the shape before measuring: `@()` around anything counted, `-join` before any whole-text operation, `[regex]` over a string made scalar on purpose — and never read a shell's convenience reshaping as the shape of the data.
61. **Settle what a flag means before writing a guard for it, and enumerate the flag surface first — the coherent mechanism may already exist and the flag may be deletable rather than fixable.** `verify-baselines.sh` accepts exactly two long options — `--results` (`:42`) and `--no-results` (`:51`) — rejects every other `--*` at `:59`, and takes one positional `ROOT_ARG` (`:64`); `:77-79` then derive `DOC`, `BASE` and `HARNESS` from that single `$ROOT` **together**. So auditing a different tree *coherently* is already supported and always was: pass the positional. `--results` is **not** the only construct in the script that can split the roots — I wrote that and it is false. `$SELF_DIR` (`:34`) is a second root, and the two checks at `:193` and `:407` assert facts about the **audited** tree while reading the **apparatus** tree: `:193` tests `$SELF_DIR/run-p05-baselines.ps1` and concludes *"the run script ships with the results it produced"*, and `:407` tests `$SELF_DIR/$script` over names `:401` derived from `$ROOT`'s document — so `:414`, the very check I proposed as the model for the fix, is itself split-rooted. Note `:74`: with no positional, `ROOT` is derived *from* `$SELF_DIR`, so the roots coincide and the split is inert — the third construct on this gate whose immunity and defect are one fact. What `--results` is, is the only construct whose split was *undisclosed*; `:145` prints `self:` beside `root:`, so this one is deliberate and announced, and it is right for **executing** the apparatus and wrong only for these two checks that read it as evidence. That reframes the fork the implementer identified. **A** — *audit the committed document against another results tree* — is a real reproducibility check, and making it coherent means moving every data root to `$RESULTS_DIR` while the document stays committed; under it, a document-derived expectation for the checkpoint set is right and a mismatch **must** fail. **B** — *audit another tree on its own terms* — is the positional argument, and needs no flag at all. The defect was never the plumbing: **the flag has never had a stated meaning, and the code implements neither reading.** This lands on me. I recorded a `:414`-shaped guard as the fix without settling which reading it enforced; under A it is correct and under B it fires on every legitimate use, so I had written a check that votes on an unsettled interface without noticing it was voting. Note also what this costs P0.6: its stated first use — gate a fresh session — is B, so it wants the positional rather than `--results`, and even that is blocked because `:77-79` hardcode `P0.5-baselines.md` and `P0.5-baselines/` into the derivation. Correction to the implementer's framing, for the record: this script has **no `--doc` flag**; `--doc` belongs to `check-prose-claims.py`, so B cannot be expressed here by pairing `--doc` with `--results`, only by the positional.
62. **Re-verify a child session when the input that arrived could plausibly change the state, not when something merely arrived.** A bare idle notification carries no content and authorizes nothing, so it is not a reason to re-run `git rev-parse`; a message asking for work is. I stated this bound twice and it was ambiguous against its own instance both times, because I wrote it as *"a new input from me"* while my own closing and declining messages are inputs that cannot authorize a commit. The purposive form terminates and the mechanical one does not: **check when the arriving input could cause the change you are checking for.** Under it, four verifications of the same no-commit instruction were three too many, and the one that mattered was the first — immediately after countermanding the child's offer to fix, which is the only moment the instruction was under live pressure.
63. **A verdict has three things it can get wrong — its contents, its extent, and its subject — and count-equality reaches only the first two.** The implementer demonstrated the third with a paired control: a copy of the tree at HEAD with `check-calibration.py` deleted, audited from *this* checkout via the positional, returns `PASS (34 checks)` exit 0 and prints `ok document names 6 script(s), 6 present, difference 0`; the same perturbed tree audited by *its own* copy of the gate returns `FAIL (32 passed, 2 failed) missing: check-calibration.py`. Same tree, same perturbation, opposite verdicts, decided only by which copy of the apparatus you invoke. Both runs carry 34 `ok` lines, so rule 59's extent assertion cannot see it and neither can rule 46 — the subset case *loses* checks, this one keeps every check and gets one **wrong**, reporting a true statement about the wrong subject. **This is the silent mis-verification I argued could not happen** when I ruled the `--results` split inert; it exists, in the construct I had just called coherent, and it took someone else building the control to produce it. The rule that follows is the split itself: **trusted apparatus, suspect artifact** — execution paths belong on `$SELF_DIR` and every assertion *about* the audited tree belongs on `$BASE`/`$ROOT`, so `:193` and `:407` are simply on the wrong side of a line the script otherwise draws correctly and discloses at `:145`. Two bounds worth carrying: coverage of the defect is **1 in 6** — only `run-p05-baselines.ps1` carries a `file:line` citation, so deleting it fails at the citation checker while both `$SELF_DIR` checks print `ok` in that same run, and the implementer's first probe hit exactly that one and nearly concluded the gate was sound; and the near-misses that preceded it were rule 54's shape twice over — four uniform `exit=127` runs where WSL could not read a worktree whose `.git` is a file, and an `exit=2` with an empty `root:` that read as gate behaviour but was a PowerShell here-string shipping CRLF into `cd $'/tmp/p05ex\r'`. Discharged against my own apparatus immediately, and it has the identical construct: `store.mjs:6-7` resolves the board with `dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url))` then `join(extensionDirectory, "roadmap.md")` — **structurally `$SELF_DIR`**, so the canvas reads the board beside whichever copy of the extension the host loaded, while my `git diff` and `Get-Content` checks read the copy I edit. Verified safe today for one reason only: exactly **one** copy of `roadmap.md` exists on this machine (`7F6BEBE5EB96`, 64 rules, in this worktree), so the two roots cannot diverge — immunity and defect as one fact for the fourth time, and the fourth is mine. The hazard is dated rather than hypothetical: **this branch is unpushed by design, and the moment it merges the main checkout gains a second copy**, after which any session outside this worktree carries its own board, the canvas renders one and my battery verifies the other, and no contents or extent check I run can tell — subject again. Honest bound on what I established: I proved there is one *candidate*, not that the host loaded it; the extension log carries no resolved-path line, so with two copies present my current checks could not discriminate at all. The guard for that day is to hash the file the host actually loaded, or to assert copy-uniqueness before trusting a reload as evidence of anything.
64. **Do not correct a claim the other party did not make.** I told the implementer that `verify-baselines.sh` has no `--doc` flag "as a correction to its framing" — true of the script, and it had never claimed otherwise: its `--doc` usage was always about `check-prose-claims.py`, and its fork message named `:288` and `:414` as the document-coupled checks without asserting any flag. I manufactured an error and then corrected it, which costs more than a silent misreading because the other party may accept authorship of a mistake that was never theirs — this one nearly did, declining only because it could not verify its own sent text and refused to accept unverifiable authorship. The check is one line: quote the sentence you are correcting before correcting it, and if you cannot find it, you are arguing with your own paraphrase.

## P0 — Parity contract, reference oracle, and measurement baseline

- **Status:** planned
- **Summary:** Establish what parity means before writing any collector code: build both candidate oracles, extract the paper's real acceptance targets, enumerate every mechanism to be ported, and capture honest built-in GC baselines.

### P0.1 — Pin and build both reference revisions

- **Status:** done
- **Summary:** Both oracle pairs built under WSL2 and verified genuinely LXR by runtime banner rather than exit code; HEAD is fully observable, PLDI is not, and the mechanism-organized diff with per-mechanism oracle recommendations and coupled sets is delivered in `docs/design/lxr-port/`.
- **Correctness:** HEAD `(0682434, 304ce69d)` passes 96/96 release runs with zero crashes or panics; PLDI `(abbdd1d, df8d30a3)` **fails outright** at 3/8 and 5/8 single-iteration and 1/8 and 2/8 sustained, tripping its own barrier assertion `assert!(old.is_null() || rc::count(old) != 0, "zero rc count")` at `plan/barriers.rs:315-319` (condition at `:316`) in `FieldLoggingBarrier::slow` — a field overwrite whose old target already has RC zero, gated by `cfg(any(sanity, debug_assertions))`, which is why release SIGSEGVs on the same corrupt state instead of panicking. The instability is **not** explained by revision skew: a differential run at core `4d4e516c` agreed with the pin in all 24 antlr/`-n 5` cells and produced the same pass set, disproving the hypothesis that the pin's `Fix stw LXR` commits were the difference. **Corrected in P0.3:** HEAD's clean runs are not evidence that the RC invariant holds there, because at `304ce69d` no barrier-side check exists at all — the only `zero rc count` assertion is in `util/sanity/sanity_checker.rs:311-316` (condition at `:312`) behind `cfg(feature = "sanity")`, which is not a default feature and was not enabled by the build recipe, so it was compiled out. The comparison was never run.
- **Benchmarks:** Reference-only numbers, no .NET comparison; recorded per configuration with invocation counts and every failure listed. Anomaly carried to P0.3 and closed there: hsqldb p99 of 0.34-0.40 ms on PLDI versus 54-56 ms on HEAD like-for-like at `-n 5` and 2000 MB, two orders of magnitude on the metric LXR exists for, from one benchmark on a noisy host, traced by P0.3 probe 2 to induced-collection policy rather than any LXR mechanism.
- **Dependencies:** none
- **References:** `docs/design/lxr-port/`; oracle pairs (`abbdd1d`, `df8d30a3`) and (`0682434`, `304ce69d`); secondary builds at core `4d4e516c` and `9625c174`, behaviorally indistinguishable; `plan/barriers.rs:315-319`; `src/args.rs` `LAZY_MU_REUSE_BLOCK_SWEEPING`

### P0.4 — Build the benchmark harness and scenario matrix

- **Status:** done
- **Summary:** Harness landed on `main` as squash merge `f6e93305259` (PR #4, 48 files, +10,994), covering all ten scenarios with a runner, worker, control suite, verification gate and gate-of-the-gate. No runtime, EE or JIT change proved necessary: effective GC configuration reads back through `GetConfigurationVariables`, tiering and PGO through `TieredCompilationSettings`, the future collector arm through `GCName`/`GCPath`, and bounded dumps through `DbgEnableMiniDump`.
- **Correctness:** Verified at the merge commit rather than at the attested tip, because the squash means `f5f1c6ed8b3` is not an ancestor of `main` and no attested hash carries. Tree identity was checked instead and holds across the whole repository, not just the harness path — the tree hashes of the attested tip and `f6e93305259` are equal, so the squash neither dropped nor swept in anything. The gate was then run from a `git archive` extract of `f6e93305259` outside any worktree: `PASS` with a full smoke results set, `exit 2` and **zero** `RESULT: PASS` lines when results are absent, `exit 2` on an empty results directory, `exit 3` and `DEGRADED` under `--no-results`, and `exit 1` naming the gap when pointed at a partial two-of-ten-scenario run. Two High review findings were fixed and regression-tested: `MeanPauseMs` triple-counted collections because `GC.CollectionCount(0)` counts gen0-or-higher, reporting 1.9306 ms against a true 3.9578 ms with a factor that varies by generation mix and so does not cancel between arms; and the bootstrap interval was zero-width at n=1, which made any ratio other than exactly 1.0 read as significant on the default smoke path.
- **Benchmarks:** No collector comparison is published here — this step builds and proves the instrument, and P0.5 measures with it. The measurement result that does bind later steps is negative: control 7 could not reliably resolve a 2% injected effect on this host, reaching the 1.6% target at n=8, at n=15, and not at all across three runs of the same binary, with direct paired probes returning 1.0221, 0.9649 and 0.9922 — a 2% signal under a ±3% single-invocation spread with the sign flipping. That is the paper's 1.6%-inside-noise problem reproduced locally. The assertion was therefore split: a coarse ~16.7% injection is asserted, a null replicate guards against manufactured effects, and the barrier-scale arm is measured and published without gating the verdict.
- **Evidence:** Run artifacts are gitignored and lived only in the child worktree, so 919 files (10.36 MB) covering `runs/`, `smoke/` and `probe/` were copied to session state before that worktree was removed, verified byte-identical by SHA256 with a negative control proving the comparison can detect a difference. Crash dumps were excluded as regenerable bulk. Without this the numbers quoted in §8 of the design document would have had no surviving source.
- **Dependencies:** none
- **References:** paper §4 methodology

### P0.5 — Measure Workstation and Server GC baselines

- **Status:** in_progress
- **Summary:** Baselines captured for both built-in collectors across the ten-scenario matrix at three heap factors, published with the raw data needed to re-derive every statistic. The step delivered what it was asked for, and what it measured is that this host cannot support the acceptance criterion as written: absolute results are not reproducible across sessions, so the comparison must move to within-session ratios.
- **Correctness:** Tested and **returned negative**, which is the step's most valuable output. 12 of 16 cells re-measured in a second session disagree beyond both their own spread and this host's measured 8.35% resolution floor — median 14.5%, max 89.6%. Decomposed rather than averaged: 6 cells had a different offered load (F23), and of the 10 comparable cells 7 still disagree. All 8 throughput comparisons moved the same direction, a 1-in-256 event under noise, tracking background load at 12.73% against 16.41%. The variance was recorded rather than averaged away, so the criterion's *method* held even as its *claim* failed.
- **Benchmarks:** `wks` and `srv` only, verified through the live canvas — 3 checkpoints, 144 collector fields, 0 naming LXR, 0 load problems. Within-session `srv`/`wks` ratio drift is 7.28% median against 19.06% for absolutes, and **three of four** throughput ratios fall below the 8.35% floor — the fourth, `long-lived-cache` at 8.74%, sits just above it while still being 3.3× more stable than its own absolute drift of 28.49%. The conclusion is unaffected: **every later step that measures LXR must do so against a baseline arm run in the same session and treat the ratio as the quantity of record** — recorded as rule 29 rather than assigned to a single step, together with the finding that the shared heap limit itself moves when LXR joins the calibration; absolute throughput here carries ±28% session-to-session, several times anything the paper reports. Throughput CV is 1.60% median with 0 of 59 cells above the floor, while p99 latency CV is 11.67% median with 34 of 60 above it — all four figures recomputed from the committed CSVs — so the quantity LXR is meant to win on is the one this host resolves worst, which sets a hard limit on what any later latency claim can assert.
- **Evidence:** PR #5 at `9f054925372`, 57 files, all under `docs/design/lxr-port/`. Verified from a `git archive` extract outside any worktree: gate `RESULT: PASS (34 checks)` exit 0 with exactly 1 anchored `^RESULT: PASS`; `--no-results` exits 3 and an unknown flag exits 2, each with 0 anchored PASS lines; control `RESULT: PASS (11 of 11 cases)` with its summary derived rather than written — "passed 2 clean extract(s), refused 1, and failed 8 single perturbation(s)". The prose checker re-derives 12 quantified claims from the shipped CSVs, and falsifying any one yields exit 1 and `1 of 12 prose claims disagree`. Eight commits past the first attestation, four of them corrections found after the step was first declared finished: a false four-ratio sentence, a set check a superset could satisfy, a gated count restated where `find_anchor` cannot see it, and a set of file counts each individually true but labelled so that two overlapping buckets read as disjoint. Three of the four were found by the child session after I had closed the step. The harness suite is now verified by me rather than reported: built from my own extract of the head with the pinned 11.0 SDK and run as a dll, giving **58 passed, 0 failed** with 58 individual pass lines. The harness subtree hashes `dfc395e68d34` identically at all six commits in the chain, so that result attaches to the head and not merely to the commit it was run at. A sixth correction removed an ungated restatement of the tie count from section 5.1's third consequence, which the session had audited and cleared on inverted grounds (rule 48); the surviving gated claim was re-perturbed with a did-it-apply guard to confirm the removal did not weaken it.
- **Corrections carried:** Two P0.4 defects found before any measurement and fixed in place at `P0.4-harness.md:90` and `:900` with the false text kept visible — a `calibrate` verb claimed twice and never written, and an inert heap axis that would have published three identically-configured unpinned runs under three different heap labels. Nothing P0.4 published was wrong, because all 528 `heapFactor` fields in its 474 preserved files are `null`; its first user would have been this step. Two further false claims were then found in this step's own document, both by me after opening the PR, and both are corrected in rule-22 form with the original visible: `:543` claimed all four throughput ratios drift below the floor when its own CSV puts `long-lived-cache` at 8.744%, and §5.1 claimed Workstation's minimum is 4 MiB against a Server range of 35–43 when the true spread is {4, 11, 19, 35, 99} against 35–139. The first passed 30 gate checks and I repeated it verbatim in the PR body; the second was written into a section added in response to my own request and survived three consecutive tips. Both are now gated, and the §5.1 fix is a merge of two commits written in parallel by the session and by me — recorded as rule 35, with the positional trap that nearly shipped the replacement ungated as rule 34.
- **Open:** `large-object-pressure` has `srv` 1.26× faster than `wks` at 88 MiB and 19× slower at 134 MiB, reproduced independently, with the `srv` side still only a hypothesis — first thing for P0.6. The blind-band assertion fired in its primary form but its bound sits 1.2× above the observed floor rather than the ~10× intended. Achieved per-arm heap factors diverge sharply from the nominal labels: at nominal 1.3x, `srv` gets 1.30–1.31x while `wks` gets 1.83–14.00x, and at 6.0x `wks` reaches 64.5x.
